citation.title: A General Method for Detecting Interference Between Units in Randomized Experiments

standing_assumptions:
Design-based (randomization) setting: $N$ units with a binary treatment vector $Z$, a finite set $\Omega$ of possible assignments, potential outcomes that are fixed numbers, and a metric of distance between units; every probability is over the random assignment. The paper states no numbered theorem or proposition; its formal content is in the introduction and the Method section. Transcribed from the page images. Printed page = PDF page + 2 (Sociological Methods & Research 41(1): 3-16).

(S1) Units, assignments, potential outcomes, p. 4 (PDF p. 2): 'In the case where the treatment status $Z$ for $N$ units is binary and $\Omega$ is the set of all possible randomizations of $Z$, SUTVA implies that potential outcomes $\{Y_{Z=0}, Y_{Z=1}\} = \{Y_{Z'=0}, Y_{Z'=1}\}, \forall Z, Z' \in \Omega$. Each potential outcome for unit $i \in \{1, 2, \ldots, N\}$ represents the outcome, $Y_i$, that would be observed if unit $i$ were in treatment condition $Z_i$.' From p. 6 on the paper writes $Y_{i,Z}$ for the outcome of unit $i$ under the assignment vector $Z$.

(S2) Design used for the exposure expectations, p. 5 (PDF p. 3): 'Consider a simple randomization of binary treatment $Z$ such that $M$ of $N$ units are assigned to treatment. These units exist on a space of arbitrary dimensionality such that we have a metric of distance between any two units $i$ and $j$.'

(S3) Fixed and variant subsets, p. 6 (PDF p. 4): 'We begin with the choice of a subset of data for which indirect effects are to be measured. This subset, which we define as the fixed subset (denoted by subscript "fixed"), can be generated by any selection process deemed appropriate by the analyst, for example, a random subset of control units, a set of "nonexperimental" units that can never be assigned to treatment, or a subset of units that share a set of common background characteristics. [...] All units not included in the fixed subset are defined to be in the variant subset (denoted by subscript "variant"). We define $S_i = 1$ if unit $i$ is fixed, $S_i = 0$ if unit $i$ is variant. For example, $Y_{variant}$ is $\{Y_j \in Y : S_j = 0\}$. As will be detailed below, any randomization inference performed will be conditional on the observed $Z_{fixed}$.'

(S4) Conditional assignment set and the null hypotheses, as printed, p. 6 (PDF p. 4): 'Let $\Omega'$ be all possible randomizations conditional on observing $Z_{fixed}$. That is, $Z_{fixed}$ is invariant for all $Z$ in $\Omega'$; $Z_i = Z_{i'}, \forall Z, Z' \in \Omega' : S_i = 1$. [...] we may define this sharp null hypothesis, $H_{0'} : Y_{i,Z} = Y_{i,Z'}, \forall i, Z' \in \Omega$. However, we are concerned with a different sharp null hypothesis: $H_{0''} : Y_{i,Z} = Y_{i,Z'}, \forall i, Z, Z' \in \Omega : Z_i = Z_{i'}$. $H_{0''}$ implies that, conditional on $Z_i$, $Y_i$ should be invariant across all randomizations—or, equivalently, that there is no interference between units.' In both conditions the prime is printed on the unit index ($Z_{i'}$); the condition meant is $Z_i = Z'_i$ (finding P030-N001, corrected in P030-T7), and every target below uses that reading. $H_{0'}$ is printed with the quantifier '$\forall i, Z' \in \Omega$'; it is read as: for all $i$ and all $Z, Z' \in \Omega$.

(S5) Test statistic, pp. 6-7 (PDF pp. 4-5): 'We define test statistic $t$ as a metric of the dependence of $Y_{fixed}$ on $Z_{variant}$. This test statistic may also be a function of any pretreatment characteristics; for example, a metric of proximity may be dependent on the density characteristics of units. This dependence is acceptable because pretreatment characteristics remain invariant across all randomizations in $\Omega$ (and thus $\Omega'$).' The statistic for a given realization of $Z$ is denoted $t_Z$ (p. 7).

(S6) Reference distribution and one-tailed $p$ value, p. 7 (PDF p. 5): 'For each $Z \in \Omega'$, a $t_0$ may be computed, such that a distribution of all $t \in T_0$, associated with $H_0$ may be constructed. [...] To determine significance, a one-tailed $p$ value, $p$ may be computed. Roughly following Rosenbaum (2002) and Ho and Imai (2006), and assuming that all $Z \in \Omega'$ occur with equal probability, $p = \Pr(t_0 \le t) = |\{t_0 \in T_0 : t_0 \le t\}| / |\Omega'|$. (2)'

(S7) The statistic the paper uses, pp. 7-8 (PDF pp. 5-6): 'we use the Spearman rank correlation coefficient, $\rho$, between $Y_{fixed}$ and $D_{nearest}$, the distance to the nearest unit of a given treatment status in the variant subset. [...] To compute $\rho$, we first compute the ranks of both random variables, $r_{D_{nearest}}$ and $r_{Y_{fixed}}$. Whenever values are tied, the average rank is used. $\rho$ then is the Pearson correlation coefficient of the ranks of these variables'. In the worked example, the simulations and the application the 'given treatment status' is treated: $D_{nearest}$ of a fixed unit is its distance to the nearest treated unit of the variant subset.

(S8) Reading conventions that are not printed and are used in the targets (definitions, not extra assumptions). (a) $Z^{obs}$ is the realized assignment and $\Omega' = \{Z \in \Omega : Z_i = Z^{obs}_i \text{ for every } i \text{ with } S_i = 1\}$. (b) Under the null, the $t_0$ belonging to $Z \in \Omega'$ is the statistic computed from the observed $Y_{fixed}$ and the assignment $Z$ (p. 10, PDF p. 8: 'in each randomization, we are assuming $H_0$, so $Y_{fixed}$ remains constant across randomizations'). (c) The numerator of (2) counts assignments in $\Omega'$, so tied statistic values keep their multiplicity (p. 10: 'Since $\rho_0 \le \rho$ in 2 of the 6 conditional randomizations, $p = 0.333$'; clarity note P030-N002). (d) 'All $Z \in \Omega'$ occur with equal probability' is the conditional law of the assignment given the selected fixed subset and its observed treatments (the reading under which candidate P030-E003 was not confirmed). (e) 'Exact' is not defined in the paper; it is read, as the validators read it, as finite-sample conditional Type I error at most $\alpha$ under the no-interference null. (f) Average ranks: the rank of $a_k$ in $(a_1, \ldots, a_n)$ is $\#\{l : a_l < a_k\} + (\#\{l : a_l = a_k\} + 1)/2$; the mean of the average ranks is $(n+1)/2$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Equation (1), corrected: the null holds the outcomes of the fixed units, not the statistic, invariant over $\Omega'$
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected sentence and display; the printed text is on p. 7 (PDF p. 5): 'it follows that we may define the salient null hypothesis $H_0 : t_Z = t_{Z'}, \forall Z, Z' \in \Omega'$. (1)'. From Sol's smallest repair and the validator's derivation (section 5).] Because the assignments in $\Omega'$ preserve the treatment statuses of the fixed units, the no-interference hypothesis implies the following null for their outcomes: $H_0 : Y_{i,Z} = Y_{i,Z'}$ for every $i$ with $S_i = 1$ and all $Z, Z' \in \Omega'$. (1) Under this null, hold the observed $Y_{fixed}$ constant and recompute the statistic for each assignment $Z$ in $\Omega'$. The statistic's reference distribution need not be constant.

[Formal content, with every hypothesis.] Setting of (S1), (S3)-(S5): a finite set $\Omega \subseteq \{0,1\}^N$ of assignments, potential outcomes $Y_{i,Z}$ for $i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$ and $Z \in \Omega$, indicators $S \in \{0,1\}^N$, a realized assignment $Z^{obs} \in \Omega$, and $\Omega' = \{Z \in \Omega : Z_i = Z^{obs}_i \text{ for every } i \text{ with } S_i = 1\}$. Write $Y_{fixed,Z} = (Y_{i,Z})_{i : S_i = 1}$. Let the statistic be $t_Z = g(Y_{fixed,Z}, Z)$ for a fixed function $g$ of the fixed units' outcome vector and the assignment (pretreatment characteristics, which do not vary over $\Omega$, are part of $g$). (a) If $H_{0''}$ holds (for all $i$ and all $Z, Z' \in \Omega$ with $Z_i = Z'_i$, $Y_{i,Z} = Y_{i,Z'}$), then the corrected $H_0$ holds. (b) If the corrected $H_0$ holds, then for every $Z \in \Omega'$, $Y_{fixed,Z} = Y_{fixed,Z^{obs}}$, the observed $Y_{fixed}$, and therefore the reference value $t_0(Z) := g(Y_{fixed,Z^{obs}}, Z)$, which is computable from the observed data, equals $t_Z$, the statistic that would have been observed under $Z$. (c) Consequently, if in addition all $Z \in \Omega'$ are equally likely, then for every real $x$, $|\{Z \in \Omega' : t_0(Z) \le x\}|/|\Omega'| = \Pr(t_Z \le x)$: the reference distribution $T_0$ is the conditional null distribution of the statistic, and the $p$ of (2) is $\Pr(t_Z \le t_{Z^{obs}})$. (d) The corrected $H_0$ does not imply $t_Z = t_{Z'}$ for $Z, Z' \in \Omega'$ (P030-T5).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [$S$, $\Omega'$, $H_{0''}$: p. 6 (PDF p. 4)] as in (S3)-(S4), with $Z_i = Z'_i$ for the misprinted $Z_i = Z_{i'}$ (P030-T7) and the reading (S8a) of $\Omega'$. [Statistic: pp. 6-7 (PDF pp. 4-5)] (S5): 'a metric of the dependence of $Y_{fixed}$ on $Z_{variant}$', possibly a function of pretreatment characteristics, which 'remain invariant across all randomizations in $\Omega$ (and thus $\Omega'$)'; $t_Z$ is 'the $t$ for a given realization of $Z$'. The function $g$ is not printed; it is the validator's way of writing that the statistic depends on the data only through the fixed units' outcomes and the assignment ($t_z = g(Y_F(z), z_{variant}, X)$ in derivation.md, section 1). [Reference values and Equation (2): p. 7] (S6), (S8b), (S8c). [Fixed outcomes under the null: p. 10 (PDF p. 8)] 'in each randomization, we are assuming $H_0$, so $Y_{fixed}$ remains constant across randomizations.'
canonical_claim.note: Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P030-E002): 'Replace the introductory inference and Equation (1) by the focal outcome null H_0: Y_{i,Z}=Y_{i,Z'} for every i with S_i=1 and every Z,Z' in Omega'. Explain that this follows from no interference because focal treatment statuses are fixed; then hold observed Y_fixed constant and recompute t for each conditional assignment.' Repair cost recorded by the validator: none; it adds no assumption beyond the no-interference null already defined, changes no estimand, and the worked example already implements it. Part (a) is the implication stated and proved in P030-T7(b); it is repeated here because the corrected sentence asserts it. Part (c) is what makes the one-tailed test valid (P030-T12). Rated Minor; listed because the author's instruction is that the corrected statement of every mathematical error is a target.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Definition of $\Omega'$ and the no-interference null $H_{0''}$, corrected ($Z_i = Z'_i$ for the printed $Z_i = Z_{i'}$), with the consequence the paper draws: dependence of $Y_{fixed}$ on $Z_{variant}$ over $\Omega'$ rejects $H_{0''}$
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed: p. 6 (PDF p. 4)] 'Let $\Omega'$ be all possible randomizations conditional on observing $Z_{fixed}$. That is, $Z_{fixed}$ is invariant for all $Z$ in $\Omega'$; $Z_i = Z_{i'}, \forall Z, Z' \in \Omega' : S_i = 1$. As Rubin (1986) notes, the sharp null hypothesis of no treatment effect is a special case of SUTVA, one in which there exists no treatment effect whatsoever (neither direct nor indirect). Roughly following Rosenbaum (2007), we may define this sharp null hypothesis, $H_{0'} : Y_{i,Z} = Y_{i,Z'}, \forall i, Z' \in \Omega$. However, we are concerned with a different sharp null hypothesis: $H_{0''} : Y_{i,Z} = Y_{i,Z'}, \forall i, Z, Z' \in \Omega : Z_i = Z_{i'}$. $H_{0''}$ implies that, conditional on $Z_i$, $Y_i$ should be invariant across all randomizations—or, equivalently, that there is no interference between units. Because $Z_{fixed} = Z'_{fixed}, \forall Z, Z' \in \Omega'$, any dependence of $Y_{fixed}$ on $Z_{variant}$, given $Z \in \Omega'$, necessarily implies that the null hypothesis of no interference between units, $H_{0''}$, must be rejected.' [Introduction, pp. 5-6 (PDF pp. 3-4)] 'Because the null hypothesis may only be false in the presence of interference, rejection of the null hypothesis is thus a sufficient condition for detection of interference.'

[Corrected, from Sol's smallest repair: replace both $Z_i = Z_{i'}$ with $Z_i = Z'_i$.] 'That is, $Z_{fixed}$ is invariant for all $Z$ in $\Omega'$; $Z_i = Z'_i, \forall Z, Z' \in \Omega' : S_i = 1$.' and '$H_{0''} : Y_{i,Z} = Y_{i,Z'}, \forall i, Z, Z' \in \Omega : Z_i = Z'_i$.'

[Formal content, with every hypothesis.] Let $\Omega \subseteq \{0,1\}^N$ be a finite set of assignments, $Y_{i,Z}$ real potential outcomes for $i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$ and $Z \in \Omega$, $S \in \{0,1\}^N$, $Z^{obs} \in \Omega$, and $\Omega' = \{Z \in \Omega : Z_i = Z^{obs}_i \text{ for every } i \text{ with } S_i = 1\}$. Corrected null: $H_{0''}$ holds when $Y_{i,Z} = Y_{i,Z'}$ for every $i$ and all $Z, Z' \in \Omega$ with $Z_i = Z'_i$. (a) For all $Z, Z' \in \Omega'$ and every $i$ with $S_i = 1$, $Z_i = Z'_i$; that is, $Z_{fixed} = Z'_{fixed}$. (b) If $H_{0''}$ holds, then for every $i$ with $S_i = 1$ and all $Z, Z' \in \Omega'$, $Y_{i,Z} = Y_{i,Z'}$: the outcomes of the fixed units do not vary over $\Omega'$. Equivalently, if there are a unit $i$ with $S_i = 1$ and $Z, Z' \in \Omega'$ with $Y_{i,Z} \ne Y_{i,Z'}$, then $H_{0''}$ is false: there are a unit and two assignments in $\Omega$ that give it the same treatment and different outcomes, which is interference between units. (c) Direct effects alone do not produce such dependence: for any real constants $c_i$ and $\tau_i$, the outcomes $Y_{i,Z} = c_i + \tau_i Z_i$ satisfy $H_{0''}$, so by (b) the outcomes of the fixed units are constant over $\Omega'$ whatever the $\tau_i$. (d) $H_{0'}$, read as $Y_{i,Z} = Y_{i,Z'}$ for every $i$ and all $Z, Z' \in \Omega$, implies $H_{0''}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Units, $\Omega$, potential outcomes: p. 4 (PDF p. 2)] (S1). [Fixed and variant subsets, $S$: p. 6 (PDF p. 4)] (S3): '$S_i = 1$ if unit $i$ is fixed, $S_i = 0$ if unit $i$ is variant'; $Z_{fixed}$ and $Y_{fixed}$ are the subvectors for units with $S_i = 1$, $Z_{variant}$ the subvector for units with $S_i = 0$. [$\Omega'$: p. 6] 'all possible randomizations conditional on observing $Z_{fixed}$', read as (S8a). [Unit index] units are indexed by $i \in \{1, 2, \ldots, N\}$ (p. 4); no unit $i'$ is defined anywhere in the paper, so the printed condition $Z_i = Z_{i'}$ has no meaning as it stands. Three lines below the first occurrence the same condition is printed with the prime on the vector: '$Z_{fixed} = Z'_{fixed}, \forall Z, Z' \in \Omega'$'. ['Dependence of $Y_{fixed}$ on $Z_{variant}$, given $Z \in \Omega'$'] read as: some fixed unit's outcome differs between two assignments in $\Omega'$ (which can differ only in $Z_{variant}$).
canonical_claim.note: P030-N001 is rated an error, Minor (a misprinted symbol in two formulas; new in this audit; confirmed in batch validation by a page check at 220 dpi, and re-read for this target on the staged page image and a 330-dpi crop): the prime sits on the subscript $i$ in both conditions. Sol's smallest repair: 'Replace both $Z_i=Z_{i'}$ with $Z_i=Z'_i$.' Repair cost: none; nothing depends on it. The target also carries the mathematical content of headline claim P030-H2 (holding the fixed units' own treatment constant, any dependence of their outcomes on the assignment of other units can only be interference, so rejection is not confounded with direct effects), which is stated in the same passage and can only be stated formally with the corrected condition; both fresh readers checked the implication (b) and found it sound. $H_{0'}$ is printed with '$\forall i, Z' \in \Omega$', without $Z$ in the quantifier; no finding was raised on it and it is read here as quantifying over both assignments. Part (b) is used in P030-T6(a) and P030-T12.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The displayed formula for $\rho$ (no square root in the denominator) and the sentence '$\rho$ has a perfect correlation coefficient (of 1 or -1) whenever $D_{nearest}$ has a monotone relationship with $Y_{fixed}$', as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 8 (PDF p. 6); Table 1 on p. 9 (PDF p. 7)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed: p. 8 (PDF p. 6)] 'To compute $\rho$, we first compute the ranks of both random variables, $r_{D_{nearest}}$ and $r_{Y_{fixed}}$. Whenever values are tied, the average rank is used. $\rho$ then is the Pearson correlation coefficient of the ranks of these variables: $\rho = \mathrm{cov}(r_{D_{nearest}}, r_{Y_{fixed}})/(\mathrm{var}(r_{D_{nearest}})\mathrm{var}(r_{Y_{fixed}}))$. $\rho$ has a perfect correlation coefficient (of 1 or -1) whenever $D_{nearest}$ has a monotone relationship with $Y_{fixed}$.' [Counterexamples from the batch validation (work/check_math.py and check_math.out.json); not in the paper.]

(a) The displayed expression is not the Pearson correlation of the ranks and does not give the paper's own values. Take the observed row of the paper's example, $D_{nearest} = (6, 1, 2, 3)$ and $Y_{fixed} = (1, 3, 2, 1)$ (p. 9). Average ranks: $r_D = (4, 1, 2, 3)$ and $r_Y = (3/2, 4, 3, 3/2)$; centred ranks $(3/2, -3/2, -1/2, 1/2)$ and $(-1, 3/2, 1/2, -1)$; sum of products $-9/2$, sums of squares $5$ and $9/2$. With moments that divide by $n = 4$: $\mathrm{cov} = -9/8$, $\mathrm{var}(r_D) = 5/4$, $\mathrm{var}(r_Y) = 9/8$, and the printed expression is $(-9/8)/((5/4)(9/8)) = -4/5$. With moments that divide by $n - 1 = 3$: $\mathrm{cov} = -3/2$, $\mathrm{var}(r_D) = 5/3$, $\mathrm{var}(r_Y) = 3/2$, and the printed expression is $(-3/2)/((5/3)(3/2)) = -3/5$. The Pearson correlation of the ranks is $(-9/2)/\sqrt{5 \cdot 9/2} = -3/\sqrt{10}$ under either divisor, which is the value the paper reports ($\rho = -0.949$, p. 9, and the last row of Table 1). Neither $-4/5$ nor $-3/5$ equals $-3/\sqrt{10}$ (their squares are $16/25$, $9/25$ and $9/10$), and the printed expression changes with the divisor convention, which a correlation does not. For the six rows of Table 1 in order the printed expression gives $-4/45, -4/45, -4/45, -20/27, -4/5, -4/5$ with divisor $n$ and $-1/15, -1/15, -1/15, -5/9, -3/5, -3/5$ with divisor $n - 1$, against the correlations $-1/\sqrt{90}, -1/\sqrt{90}, -1/\sqrt{90}, -5/6, -3/\sqrt{10}, -3/\sqrt{10}$ that round to the printed $-0.105, -0.105, -0.105, -0.833, -0.949, -0.949$.

(b) The printed expression can order two distance vectors differently from the correlation. With $Y_{fixed} = (1, 3, 2, 1)$ and divisor $n$: for $D_A = (1, 2, 1, 1)$ (ranks $(2, 4, 2, 2)$) the correlation is $\sqrt{6}/3$ and the printed expression is $8/9$; for $D_B = (0, 2, 1, 1)$ (ranks $(1, 4, 5/2, 5/2)$) the correlation is $5/6$ and the printed expression is $20/27$. Thus $\rho_A < \rho_B$ (squares $2/3 < 25/36$) while the printed expression is larger for $A$ ($8/9 = 24/27 > 20/27$).

(c) A monotone relationship without perfect rank correlation. Let $D = (1, 2, 3)$ and $Y = (0, 0, 1)$: $Y$ is a nondecreasing, nonconstant function of $D$. Average ranks $r_D = (1, 2, 3)$ and $r_Y = (3/2, 3/2, 3)$; centred ranks $(-1, 0, 1)$ and $(-1/2, -1/2, 1)$; sum of products $3/2$, sums of squares $2$ and $3/2$; $\rho = (3/2)/\sqrt{2 \cdot 3/2} = \sqrt{3}/2 \approx 0.866$, which is neither $1$ nor $-1$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Average ranks: p. 8 (PDF p. 6)] 'Whenever values are tied, the average rank is used', with the formula (S8f). [Pearson correlation of the ranks] for rank vectors $r_D$, $r_Y$ of length $n$ with common mean $\bar r = (n+1)/2$: $\sum_k (r_{D,k} - \bar r)(r_{Y,k} - \bar r)\big/\sqrt{\sum_k (r_{D,k} - \bar r)^2\sum_k (r_{Y,k} - \bar r)^2}$, defined when neither vector is constant. [cov, var] not defined in the paper; both usual conventions are checked: $\mathrm{cov}(a, b) = \frac{1}{m}\sum_k (a_k - \bar a)(b_k - \bar b)$ and $\mathrm{var}(a) = \mathrm{cov}(a, a)$ with $m = n$ or with $m = n - 1$. [Monotone relationship] not defined in the paper; in (c) it is read as weakly monotone: $Y$ is a nondecreasing function of $D$. [Example data: p. 9 (PDF p. 7)] $Y_{fixed} = \{1, 3, 2, 1\}$, $D_{nearest} = \{6, 1, 2, 3\}$, $\rho = -0.949$, and Table 1 as transcribed in P030-T14.
canonical_claim.note: P030-E004 is rated an error, Minor (a misprint: the formula lacks the square root, and the remark on perfect correlation needs 'strictly' monotone); the batch validator's verdict is confirmed in part. The same sentence names the Pearson correlation of the ranks and Table 1 uses it, so no reported value changes; the rating records no headline claim as affected (the claim named here is the one the statistic serves). Parts (a) and (c) are the two halves of the finding; (b) is the validator's illustration that a literal implementation could change randomization orderings when distance ties vary, and is a statement about the statistic, not about the paper's simulations. Not established: that the printed expression fails to be invariant under monotone transformations of the raw data (it still depends on the data only through ranks). The weak-monotonicity example does not refute the sentence if 'monotone' is read as strictly monotone; the corrected statement is P030-T9. All numbers in (a)-(c) were recomputed in exact rational arithmetic in writing this target. The printed formula is not listed as a separate as-printed target because the finding is below Moderate.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The formula for $\rho$ and the sentence on perfect correlation, corrected: square root in the denominator; $|\rho| = 1$ exactly when the centred rank vectors are proportional
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected, from Sol's smallest repair; the printed text is on p. 8 (PDF p. 6) and is quoted in P030-T8.] $\rho = \mathrm{cov}(r_{D_{nearest}}, r_{Y_{fixed}})\big/\sqrt{\mathrm{var}(r_{D_{nearest}})\,\mathrm{var}(r_{Y_{fixed}})}$. With nonconstant ranks, $|\rho| = 1$ exactly when the centered rank vectors are proportional; a strictly monotone relationship preserving or reversing ties suffices. Weak monotonicity alone need not suffice.

[Formal content, with every hypothesis.] Let $n \ge 2$ and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}^n$, neither of them constant. Let $r(a)_k = \#\{l : a_l < a_k\} + (\#\{l : a_l = a_k\} + 1)/2$ be the average ranks, and likewise $r(b)$; both have mean $(n+1)/2$. Write $\tilde r(a) = r(a) - (n+1)/2$ and $\tilde r(b) = r(b) - (n+1)/2$ for the centred rank vectors (both nonzero), and define $\rho(a, b) = \sum_k \tilde r(a)_k \tilde r(b)_k \big/ \sqrt{\sum_k \tilde r(a)_k^2 \sum_k \tilde r(b)_k^2}$. (i) Divisor: $\rho(a, b) = \mathrm{cov}(r(a), r(b))/\sqrt{\mathrm{var}(r(a))\mathrm{var}(r(b))}$ whether the covariance and variances divide by $n$ or by $n - 1$. (ii) $-1 \le \rho(a, b) \le 1$. (iii) $|\rho(a, b)| = 1$ if and only if there is a real $c \ne 0$ with $\tilde r(a) = c\,\tilde r(b)$; then $\rho(a, b) = 1$ if $c > 0$ and $\rho(a, b) = -1$ if $c < 0$. (iv) If for all $k, l$: $a_k < a_l$ if and only if $b_k < b_l$ (a strictly increasing relationship that preserves ties), then $r(a) = r(b)$ and $\rho(a, b) = 1$. (v) If for all $k, l$: $a_k < a_l$ if and only if $b_k > b_l$ (a strictly decreasing relationship that preserves ties), then $r(a)_k = n + 1 - r(b)_k$ for every $k$ and $\rho(a, b) = -1$. (vi) Weak monotonicity is not enough: $a = (1, 2, 3)$, $b = (0, 0, 1)$ has $\rho(a, b) = \sqrt{3}/2$ (P030-T8(c)). (vii) With this formula the six rows of Table 1 ($b = Y_{fixed} = (1, 3, 2, 1)$ and $a = D_{nearest}$ equal to $(1,6,7,8)$, $(2,5,6,7)$, $(3,4,5,6)$, $(4,3,4,5)$, $(5,2,3,4)$, $(6,1,2,3)$) give $-1/\sqrt{90}$, $-1/\sqrt{90}$, $-1/\sqrt{90}$, $-5/6$, $-3/\sqrt{10}$, $-3/\sqrt{10}$, which round to the printed $-0.105$, $-0.105$, $-0.105$, $-0.833$, $-0.949$, $-0.949$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Ranks and $\rho$: p. 8 (PDF p. 6)] 'To compute $\rho$, we first compute the ranks of both random variables, $r_{D_{nearest}}$ and $r_{Y_{fixed}}$. Whenever values are tied, the average rank is used. $\rho$ then is the Pearson correlation coefficient of the ranks of these variables'. [cov, var] not defined in the paper; $\mathrm{cov}(a, b) = \frac{1}{m}\sum_k (a_k - \bar a)(b_k - \bar b)$, $\mathrm{var}(a) = \mathrm{cov}(a, a)$, with $m = n$ or $m = n - 1$. [Nonconstant] a vector is constant when all its entries are equal; then all its average ranks equal $(n+1)/2$, its centred rank vector is zero and $\rho$ is undefined. The paper does not say what the statistic is in that case. [Table 1: p. 9 (PDF p. 7)] as transcribed in P030-T14.
canonical_claim.note: Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P030-E004), quoted in the first paragraph of the statement. Repair cost: none. The validator's justification of (iii) is the equality case of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for nonzero centred rank vectors. In (iv) and (v) the stated condition forces $a_k = a_l$ exactly when $b_k = b_l$, which is what 'preserving or reversing ties' means; (v) uses $\#\{l : a_l < a_k\} = \#\{l : b_l > b_k\}$ and $\#\{l : b_l < b_k\} + \#\{l : b_l = b_k\} + \#\{l : b_l > b_k\} = n$. Part (vii) is the check, made by both fresh readers and the validators, that the worked table uses the corrected formula. Rated Minor; listed because the author's instruction is that the corrected statement of every mathematical error is a target.

canonical_claim.note: P030-E006 is rated an error, Minor (batch validation: confirmed): the kernel $1/(1.5d)^2$ is called exponential on pp. 10-11 and in Figure 2, and its sum is written without excluding $j = i$. Sol's smallest repair is quoted in the statement; repair cost: none. No reported simulation rate is shown to change, and nothing establishes that the simulation code evaluated a self term; the misnaming matters for what the robustness claim covers (no exponential decay was simulated). Caution for the formalizer: in Lean with Mathlib, division by zero is defined to be zero, so the printed summand evaluates to $0$ there and the printed and corrected sums coincide; that convention is not the paper's arithmetic, and the target is the corrected definition with the sum over $j \ne i$ (statement (i) about the printed summand is a remark on real arithmetic, to be recorded in a docstring and not proved as a Lean theorem about division). The Gaussian and linear models carry the same factor $(1 - \delta_{ij})$ but their self terms are defined (the factor makes them zero), so only the third model needs the change. The validator also records the logarithmic derivative $-2/d$ and that the lower-left panel of Figure 2 agrees with $k$ at $d = 2/3, 1, 2$. Rated Minor; listed because the correction changes a printed formula and the author's instruction covers every such error. The headline claim named is the simulation claim the model belongs to; that claim is not itself a target.
